newsitem.title: USA: TALKING POINT/Viacom's Blockbuster H2 seen better.
newsitem.headline: TALKING POINT/Viacom's Blockbuster H2 seen better.

text.p: Viacom Inc, which suffered a sharp loss in the second quarter due to a $323 million charge at its ailing Blockbuster unit, could see second-half improvement at the video renter, analysts said Tuesday.
"It's too early to tell, but indications are somewhat positive," said David Doft, an analyst at Furman Selz.
Analysts said Blockbuster's performance may be helped in the second half by the video release of a slew of movies that were popular at the box office.
Also, comparisons to last year should improve because 1996 video rentals dropped as viewers chose to watch the summer Olympics in Atlanta.

"Sales growth has seen a pickup," said Jill Krutick, an analyst at Smith Barney. "(Blockbuster) faces easy comparisons compared to a year ago, heading into the third quarter, due to better products and the Olympics a year ago."

Analysts said it is still too early to judge the performance of John Antioco, who was named to run Blockbuster in June. They said completion of a new distribution center is still expected late in the first quarter of 1998.
Ed Hatch at UBS Securities said he expected Blockbuster to generate $450-$500 million in cash flow for the year compared with $773 million last year.

Viacom lost $217 million in the second quarter, including the Blockbuster charge -- for store closings and writedown of excess video inventory -- versus a profit $26 million. Cash flow fell to $127 million from $472 million a year ago.

Other Viacom units performed well, especially networks and broadcasting, analysts said. "The quarter came in slightly better than my pessimistic expectations," said Krutick. "Every business did slightly better out of the block."
Analysts said results at the MTV cable networks were strong, and in line with estimates. MTV cash flow rose 15 percent to $127 million in the second quarter.
Hatch said cash flow for the Showtime cable network rose to $27 million from $17 million, due to lower programming costs and getting out of the TV satellite dish business.

Investors have been unhappy at the company's debt -- which was $10.7 billion at June 30 -- and the lagging stock price, which topped $53 in September 1995, was $42 in May 1996 and has hovered around the mid-to-low $30s this year.

Krutick said investors still look at Viacom as a "show-me stock. It's going to take some time for people to believe that improvement at Blockbuster is sustainable and that the longer-term strategy is on the right course."
